faqs.q: How do I convert my hourly rate to an annual salary?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work per week, then multiply by 52 weeks. For a standard full-time role, we assume 38 hours per week. For example, $26.44 per hour × 38 hours × 52 weeks = $52,254 per year. If you work fewer or more hours, adjust the weekly figure accordingly. This is your gross annual pay before tax and super.

faqs.q: What is casual loading and how does it affect my pay?
faqs.a: Casual loading is an extra 25% paid on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave (such as annual leave and sick leave). From 1 July 2026, the casual rate for an adult award-free employee is $33.05 per hour ($26.44 base + 25%). When using our calculator, do not type a rate that already includes casual loading; instead, check the casual loading box and enter your base rate.

faqs.q: How is superannuation calculated and is it included in my take-home pay?
faqs.a: Superannuation is paid by your employer on top of your ordinary earnings at a rate of 12% (from 1 July 2026). It is not deducted from your salary – it is an additional contribution to your retirement fund. For example, on a gross salary of $52,254, your employer would contribute an extra $6,270 in super, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. Super does not appear in your take-home pay because it goes directly into your super account.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding Your Take Home Pay: From Hourly Rate to Annual Salary

If you’re used to a **take home pay calculator UK** style, you might expect a simple hourly-to-annual conversion. But Australian workers need to account for our unique system: award rates, casual loading, superannuation paid on top, and a progressive tax scale with Medicare. This guide explains how to convert your hourly rate to an annual figure, what the National Minimum Wage means, and how to estimate your take-home pay.

### The Basic Formula

The core calculation is straightforward: **hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks**. For a full-time employee, we assume a standard 38-hour week, as defined by the Fair Work Commission. If you work part-time or casual, use your actual weekly hours.

For example, the National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour. Multiply by 38 hours gives $1,004.90 per week, and by 52 weeks gives $52,254.80 per year. This is your gross annual salary before tax and super.

### National Minimum Wage and Award Rates

The Fair Work Commission sets the National Minimum Wage each year. From 1 July 2026, it is $26.44 per hour for adult award-free employees. However, many workers are covered by an award or enterprise agreement that specifies higher minimum rates. The Fair Work Ombudsman provides a [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) guide and a Pay Calculator to check your exact rate.

### Casual Loading

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave. The casual rate for the National Minimum Wage is $33.05 per hour ($26.44 + 25%). When using our [timesheet](/), do **not** enter a rate that already includes casual loading. Instead, enter your base hourly rate and tick the casual loading checkbox – the calculator will add the 25% automatically.

### Superannuation Paid on Top

Superannuation is an employer contribution of 12% of your ordinary earnings (from 1 July 2026). It is paid **on top** of your gross salary, not deducted from it. For a full-time worker on $52,254, the employer adds $6,270 to your super fund each year, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. Super does not appear in your take-home pay because it goes directly to your super account. Learn more about [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging).

### Tax and Medicare

Your take-home pay is your gross salary minus tax and the Medicare levy. For the 2026–27 financial year, the resident tax rates are:

- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Medicare levy is generally 2% of taxable income, with reductions for low-income earners (using 2025–26 thresholds as 2026–27 thresholds are not yet confirmed). Our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) estimator applies these rates to give you a net figure.

### Fortnightly Pay

Many Australian employers pay fortnightly. To find your fortnightly gross pay, simply multiply your weekly pay by two. For the National Minimum Wage: $1,004.90 per week × 2 = $2,009.80 per fortnight. After tax and Medicare, your take-home will be less.

### What This Calculator Does and Doesn’t Do

Our calculator assumes you work the same number of hours every week, with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, allowances, or salary sacrifice. It uses the 2026–27 tax scale and the 12% super guarantee. It does not deduct HELP repayments, the Medicare levy surcharge, or salary packaging. Always check your specific circumstances with the Fair Work Ombudsman or a qualified adviser.

### Why a UK-Style Calculator Isn’t Enough

A **take home pay calculator UK** uses British tax bands, National Insurance, and no compulsory superannuation like Australia’s. Australian workers need a tool that reflects our award system, casual loading, and super paid on top. Our calculator is designed for Australian conditions, using official Fair Work and ATO data.

### Using the Timesheet

To get started, visit our [timesheet](/). Enter your base hourly rate, select your hours per week (default 38), and check the casual loading box if applicable. The calculator will show your annual gross, super, and estimated take-home pay after tax and Medicare.

### Summary

- **Annual gross** = hourly rate × hours per week × 52
- **National Minimum Wage** (2026–27): $26.44/hr, $1,004.90/week
- **Casual loading**: 25% on top of base rate
- **Super**: 12% paid on top of ordinary earnings, up to $270,830
- **Tax**: progressive rates from 0% to 45% plus 2% Medicare
- **Fortnightly**: multiply weekly by 2

Use our [average pay](/topics/average-pay) page to compare your rate with ABS data, or check [job pay](/topics/job-pay) for award-specific rates. Remember, this is an estimate – always verify with official sources.
